title: Polycrisis Resilience While Conditions Worsen Over Centuries
subtitle: Human and Systemic Vulnerability Reduction Under Long-Term Environmental, Economic, and Geopolitical Deterioration

contribution: Introduces Long-Horizon Polycrisis Resilience—originated by Hunter Hughes, Founder of H Heuristics—connecting Temporal, Developmental, and Environmental resilience across five analytical horizons (2025–2500+) and four deterioration categories (preventable, mitigable, persistent, and adaptive conditions).
keywords: Polycrisis Resilience While Conditions Worsen Over Centuries
abstract:
Polycrisis Resilience While Conditions Worsen Over Centuries is a foundational publication within the H Heuristics Polycrisis Resilience Series, based on the concept developed by Hunter Hughes, Founder of H Heuristics (https://polycrisisresilience.hheuristics.com/).
It extends Polycrisis Resilience across century-scale and multicentury horizons (2025–2500+), introducing the concept of Long-Horizon Polycrisis Resilience and examining how technological progress, sustainable development in the Global South, and intergenerational institutions preserve human well-being even when baseline planetary conditions deteriorate.

keyFindings.title: Resilience must be developed relative to changing baseline conditions, including scenarios in which the operating baseline itself becomes progressively less favorable over centuries; a society can recover from discrete disasters while becoming more vulnerable overall.

Long-Horizon Polycrisis Resilience connects Temporal, Developmental, and Environmental resilience—measuring success by whether future generations inherit lower vulnerability and stronger adaptive institutions across 2025–2050, 2050–2100, 2100–2200, and 2200–2500+.

Distinguishing Preventable, Mitigable, Persistent, and Adaptive deterioration prevents the framework from assuming every underlying trend can be reversed, focusing capital on durable functionality even under unfavorable environmental baselines.

Technological advancement, economic convergence, and institutional knowledge transmission act as powerful countervailing forces, compressing long-horizon vulnerability from 65.0 (2025) to 19.0 by 2100 and 12.0 by 2500 (-81.5%) versus 98.5 under unmitigated deterioration.
